rashi:a1.1: “That may you offer for a gift [nedava]”: and we say below (Temurah 7b) that this refers to items consecrated for Temple maintenance. And one can infer [from the word otó, “it”]: “it” you may assign to Temple maintenance, but you may not assign unblemished animals to Temple maintenance.
rashi:a1.2: With a prohibition: as we expound below: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying [lemor]” — [read it as] lo emor, “do not say” [that is, do not declare them consecrated].
rashi:a2.1: From the place that blemished animals are included for the altar: that they become consecrated after the fact.
rashi:a2.2: Are included etc.: for in that very verse it is written, “But for a vow it shall not be accepted,” and we say below (Temurah 7b) that this refers to items consecrated for the altar. And it is written “it shall not be accepted,” implying that they do not effect acceptance, but if one consecrates them, they are consecrated. And unblemished animals for Temple maintenance are juxtaposed to blemished animals for the altar, since both come from one verse for the prohibition that one may not consecrate [them]. Therefore they are juxtaposed also with regard to “what he did is done.”
rashi:a3.1: According to the time of the robbery: [the value of] plain wool and wood; but the vessels and the garments he acquired through the change. Evidently [the transgression] is effective.
rashi:a4.1: “That he took by robbery”: [he returns it only if it is] like what he robbed.
rashi:a5.1: And Abaye: [holds that the verse] is not needed for this, since I already know that [a transgression] is effective; rather, it is for this exposition. This “that he took by robbery” is written in connection with an oath that he swore falsely, and it is written (Leviticus 5) “he shall add a fifth.” It teaches us that for his own robbery he adds a fifth, if he swore falsely and then admitted.
rashi:a5.2: But he does not add a fifth for his father’s robbery: even if he swore falsely about it.
rashi:a6.1: He returns the mattress at night etc.: this is taught in Bava Metzia, in chapter HaMekabel (Bava Metzia 113a), with regard to one who takes collateral against the debtor’s will. Evidently it is effective, and he acquires the collateral: an item for the day, that is, the plow, the creditor acquires at night, and a covering for the night the creditor acquires by day. Evidently it is effective.
rashi:a7.1: It is different there, as it is written: “You shall restore [hashev teshivenu] to him”: from the amplification of the verse we derive that he returns it many times, and that can only be found in this way: he returns an item for the day by day and an item for the night at night. And from here we derive that he acquires [it]. And for Abaye, the amplification of the verse does not imply this, and hashev teshivenu is needed, since if it were not written I would say: if he wants, he returns it, and if he wants, he does not return it.
rashi:a7.2: This is the version we read: Another version: Rava could say to you: It is different there, as it is written, “Until the sun goes down you shall restore it.” And we expound it in [chapter] HaMekabel thus: all day, until the sun sets, you shall restore it to the borrower, and when the sun sets you shall take it from him. From here [we learn] about a garment for the day, that it is given to be taken as collateral at night. And another verse is written: “You shall restore the pledge when the sun goes down” — from here [we learn] about a garment for the night, that it is given to be taken as collateral by day. And from here we derive that it is effective. And Abaye could say to you: [these verses come] not to teach us that it is effective, but rather one for a garment for the day, that he must return it by day, and one for a garment for the night, that he is obligated to return it at night; and both are necessary. And this “both are necessary” was not explained to us. It seems to me that it is thus: had it taught us about an item for the day, such as a plow, [I would say that is] because it is his livelihood, but a covering for the night, I would say not; and had it written a covering for the night, [I would say that is] because he suffers [without it], but a covering for the day, I would say not.
rashi:a9.1: He smoothed it [meiraḥo]: it has become fixed [as obligated] for tithe and for teruma.
rashi:a10.1: He tithes: first, and afterward he gives the pe’a.
rashi:a10.2: A conclusive refutation of Abaye: who said [a transgression] is effective, for here it is not effective.
rashi:a11.1: “You shall leave,” “you shall leave”: “You shall leave them for the poor and for the stranger” is written twice, once in [the portion of] Kedoshim Tihyu and once in Emor el HaKohanim, to teach us from the superfluous “you shall leave” that even though it changed in his hand, he did not acquire it.
rashi:a13.1: He is obligated in peret and olelot etc.: even though ownerless property is exempt from all of these, ownerless property like this is obligated. We derive this from the superfluous “you shall leave,” since with all of them the superfluous “you shall leave” is written.
rashi:a13.2: And exempt from tithe: for with tithe the superfluous “you shall leave” is not written. And the [extra] “you shall leave” comes to include this ownerless property, and not to include a change, for in general too [according to Rava, a transgression] is not effective.
rashi:a14.1: And now that we have given all these answers: that there are cases where it is effective and cases where it is not effective, and in all of them Abaye and Rava agree — with regard to what do they disagree?
tosafot:a3.1: He pays according to the time of the robbery: for a change acquires; evidently it is effective, and it is a refutation of Rava.
tosafot:a6.1: He returns the mattress at night and the plow by day, and it is a refutation of Rava: for if it were not effective, his seizure would not be a valid seizure, and he would have to return them to the owners entirely. And if you say: from where do we know [that the mishna speaks of one who transgressed]? Perhaps it speaks of one who took collateral with permission, that is, the court’s agent took the collateral, and of him it says that he returns the mattress at night and the plow by day, since he did not transgress; but where he transgressed, I would say that it is not effective. One can say that this mishna is taught in chapter HaMekabel (Bava Metzia 113a) with regard to one who took collateral without permission, for just before it, it teaches: One who lends to another may take collateral from him only through the court, and he may not enter his house to take his collateral, as it is stated: “You shall stand outside.” If he had two items, he takes one and leaves one; he returns the mattress at night and the plow by day. Evidently it refers to [collateral taken] without permission.
tosafot:a7.1: In brief: Tosafot ask from Bava Metzia 31b, where “hashev tashiv” is expounded to include collateral taken without permission. That implies that without the verse, such collateral would not need to be returned at all, whereas here, for Rava, without the verse the seizure would be void and returned entirely. They answer that for Rava the baraita there means: from where do we know that he returns it and takes it back, i.e., that the seizure takes effect? And for Abaye it means: from where do we know that he must return it at all, since the act was effective? That fits our Gemara, which says that for Abaye, without the verse he might return it or not as he wished. They then ask from the end of chapter HaMekabel (Bava Metzia 116a), where Abaye told a man who had taken a knife (sakina de’ashkavta) as collateral, “Go return it,” since it is among the items used to prepare food: if for Abaye the act is effective, why return it? They answer that the man there did not intend to transgress. This also settles the mishna in Bava Metzia 115a that one who takes a mill and an upper millstone as collateral receives two sets of lashes, although for Abaye the prohibition can be remedied by returning the item: the lashes are where he intended to transgress. Others answer that the lashes are where the item was lost and cannot be returned; Tosafot reject this, since the last chapter of Makkot (16b) implies that where the man is able to pay, the nullification does not help. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a10.1: He separates even from the dough: and a change of name does not acquire [here].
tosafot:a11.1: In brief: Tosafot ask that here Abaye needs the extra “you shall leave” and Rava does not, while at the start of HaGozel Etzim (Bava Kamma 94a) it is the reverse: Abaye proves from this statement of Rabbi Yishmael that a change does not acquire, and Rava rejects the proof because the extra “you shall leave” is written. They answer that our Gemara speaks according to the first tanna. For Abaye, without the extra verse one who transgressed “you shall not wholly reap” would not have to separate pe’a at all; but according to the first tanna, once the grain changed in his hand into dough he acquired it through the change and need not separate pe’a from then on. Rabbi Yishmael, who has him separate even from the dough, holds that a change does not acquire, and the extra verse is still needed for grain that has not changed: although in general a transgression is effective, here it is not. For Rava, who holds that a transgression is not effective, the first tanna needs no extra verse to require pe’a after the transgression, and once the grain changed he is exempt, since a change acquires; and Rabbi Yishmael holds that a change acquires in general but not here, because of the extra “you shall leave.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a13.1: One who renounced ownership of his vineyard, and rose early in the morning and harvested it, is obligated in peret, olelot, forgotten clusters and pe’a: Rashi explained: even though ownerless property is exempt from all of these, ownerless property like this is obligated, and we derive it from the superfluous “you shall leave,” since with all of them the superfluous “you shall leave” is written. And the Ri says that the obligation applies where he acquired the field itself; but where he acquired only the fruit, he is exempt from all of them.
tosafot:a14.1: And now that we have given all these answers, with regard to what do Abaye and Rava disagree?: And if you say: let us say they disagree in a case like this: a man who swore not to divorce his wife and afterward transgressed and divorced her — for Abaye it is effective, and for Rava the divorce is not effective, since he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One. One can say: since the prohibition is not like “he may not send her away all his days,” but rather he invented the prohibition himself, in such a case Rava did not say that it is not effective. And Rabbeinu Barukh found it difficult: why does it not say that they disagree in this case, for example, where one redeemed a firstborn, or tithe, or dedicated property? It is not effective according to everyone, as the passage explains; so for Abaye he is not flogged, since it is not effective, for so Abaye said above, that where it is not effective, he is not flogged; and for Rava he is flogged, because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One. This requires further study.
gershom:a1.1: “It”: [The printed edition’s note: It seems one should read: as it is written, “too long or too short… that may you offer for a gift,” and these are blemished animals, as explained in Bekhorot; and we expound: “it” you may consecrate, but you may not consecrate unblemished animals for Temple maintenance. End of the comment.] Too long or too short are blemished animals, as explained in Bekhorot: those you consecrate for Temple maintenance, and not unblemished ones [which are] for the altar. [The printed edition’s note: One should read: from this verse, “that may you offer for a gift,” and blemished animals were included for the altar, as it is written “but for a vow it shall not be accepted,” unblemished animals were also included for Temple maintenance. This belongs to the next comment.] And from that same verse unblemished animals were also included for Temple maintenance, through the juxtaposition: for from this verse too, “that may you offer for a gift… but for a vow it shall not be accepted,” blemished animals were included for the altar, as it is written “but for a vow it shall not be accepted.”
gershom:a2.1: Rava could say to you: it is different here. For from the place that blemished animals were included for the altar, as it is written, “but for a vow it shall not be accepted” — it is effecting acceptance, being sacrificed, that they do not do, but if one consecrates them they are consecrated — [unblemished animals were also included for Temple maintenance]. And unblemished animals for Temple maintenance are juxtaposed to blemished animals for the altar: just as with blemished animals for the altar we say that even though it is [done] with a prohibition, what he did is done, so too with unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, even though it is with a prohibition, what he did is done.
gershom:a3.1: He pays according to the time of the robbery: and not as they are now. Since he does not pay as they are now but according to the time of the robbery, evidently it is effective.
gershom:a4.1: This “that he took by robbery” comes for this: that for his own robbery he adds a fifth, and not for what his father robbed.
gershom:a5.1: But there is collateral etc.: [evidently, since he returns the mattress not by day but only at night, and the plow only by day,] learn from it that if one did it, it is effective, and he acquired it as collateral, for he returns [the mattress] only at night, and by day he goes back and takes it.
gershom:a6.1: Rava could say to you: it is different there: for there we find explicitly that he acquires; since it was necessary to write “hashev tashiv,” learn from it that this is because he acquires the collateral. Another version: since it is written “until the sun goes down” — like “until the Jubilee year” — from sunrise until the sun goes down you shall return it to him, and not before; by implication, he acquires collateral for the day [the plow] at night. And since it is written, “You shall restore [the pledge] to him when the sun goes down” [that is, at sunset] and not before, by implication he acquires collateral for the night [the mattress] by day, for all day the mattress belongs to the creditor until sunset.
gershom:a7.1: And Abaye holds: they come only, one for a covering for the day and one for a covering for the night, and it is necessary to learn that for both he must return it to him.
gershom:a8.1: He smoothed it [meraḥo]: he leveled the surface of the pile, and its work was completed with respect to tithe; it is forbidden for anyone to eat until he tithes. Therefore he tithes, and afterward gives him pe’a.
gershom:a9.1: He separates even from the dough: before its ḥalla was taken. And therefore, once it has become obligated in ḥalla, he separates [its ḥalla and gives pe’a].
gershom:a10.1: A refutation of Abaye: for evidently it is not effective; rather, he is obligated to give in any case.
gershom:a11.1: “You shall leave,” “you shall leave” [azov ta’azov]: for it could have said “leave [azov] for the poor and for the stranger”; why “you shall leave [ta’azov]”? It includes: in any case.
gershom:a12.1: He is obligated in peret, olelot, forgotten clusters and pe’a: for with all of these “you shall leave” is written, which includes even ownerless property.
gershom:a13.1: And exempt from tithe: since “you shall leave” is not written with it.
gershom:a14.1: [And now that we have given all these answers, “Rava could say to you,” “Abaye could say to you,” with regard to what do they disagree? They disagree] with regard to fixed interest. For Abaye, who said that if one did it, it is effective, he does not return [it].
gershom:a15.1: Another version: they disagree with regard to fixed interest, and in line with Rabbi Elazar etc. [He said to him:] No, [there] they disagree about verses: “He has given forth upon interest, and has taken increase; shall he then live? He shall not live” — [his blood is upon him: it was given for death and not for returning]. This is the reason of Abaye and Rava [so the printed text], who hold that it is repossessed by the judges: because the verse is written, [“Take no interest of him or increase, but fear your God, that your brother may live with you”] — return to him the interest, which you should not take from him, so that he may live with you.
rashi:b1.1: A hint of interest [avak ribbit]: that which comes through a sale, for example one who sells his field and says: If you give me [the money] now, it is yours for a thousand zuz, and if at the threshing floor [i.e., later], for twelve maneh [twelve hundred]. And they disagree about fixed interest: Abaye, who says it is effective, [holds] like Rabbi Yoḥanan, and Rava like Rabbi Elazar, for here there is no verse either way.
rashi:b2.1: There do they disagree with regard to logical reasoning?: He says it as a question of astonishment. There they disagree with regard to verses etc.
rashi:b2.2: It was given for life: that is to say, that he shall not live, and not for returning. And even for Rava it is effective, since a verse is written.
rashi:b6.1: With regard to whether a change acquires [Rashi’s text reads shinui koneh, “a change acquires”; the Davidson renders it “whether deviation is effective”]: for Abaye holds that a change by which one changed and transgressed the will of the Omnipresent acquires, except where verses are written; and for Rava it does not acquire, except where verses are written. And it is not explained to us that there is any [practical difference] between them, only the answers to these refutations: one Sage holds that it is because it is effective or not effective, and the other Sage holds that it is because of the reasoning of the verses. [A further remark, marked נ״ב:] We could say [that they differ] with regard to whether a change acquires, for example one who robbed wood and made it into vessels, or wool and made it into garments: for Abaye he acquired them and pays only for wood and wool, and for Rava he did not acquire them and pays the garments and the vessels. And when we challenged Rava above from what is taught, “One who robs wood and fashions it into vessels etc.,” [he would] not say “it is different there, as it is written ‘that he took by robbery’”; rather, he would say: I hold like the one who says a change does not acquire. For this is a dispute in Bava Kamma, chapter Merubba (Bava Kamma 66a) and in the first [chapter] HaGozel (ibid. 94a): there is one who says a change acquires and derives the reason from “that he took by robbery,” like what he robbed; and there is one who says a change does not acquire and derives it from “and he shall restore the stolen item,” in any case. If so, why does the verse state “that he took by robbery”? To say that he does not add a fifth for his father’s robbery.
rashi:b6.2: This is the reading we have: “Another version: with regard to these answers that we answered.” And between this version and the version I heard, “with regard to whether a change acquires,” there is no difference, except that one is a “Jerusalem” [reading] and the other a “Babylonian” one.
rashi:b10.1: The Sages taught: If [it is for] “you may not slaughter,” that is already stated below: that one may not slaughter a blemished animal for the altar; and further on it explains it. And burning too, and sprinkling its blood, are explained further on.
rashi:b10.2: If so, why does the verse state “you shall not offer”? [To teach:] you shall not consecrate.
rashi:b10.3: Five categories: further on it derives them.
rashi:b10.4: One who consecrates blemished animals: and burned them all as a burnt offering.
rashi:b13.1: These are fires: the burning of the sacrificial portions.
rashi:b14.1: To include the scapegoat: that one who consecrates it blemished is flogged on account of “you shall not consecrate.”
rashi:b15.1: “Offering”: written with regard to slaughtering outside: “and has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting… to present it as an offering unto the Lord.”
rashi:b15.2: This is the reading: “If ‘offering,’ I would derive etc.”: it refers back to what is above in Torat Kohanim, which teaches above: One might think that one who slaughters non-sacred animals inside [the Temple] is liable; the verse states “offering”: for an offering he is liable, and he is not liable for non-sacred animals. “If ‘offering,’ I would derive etc.,” that is to say: if you expound “offering,” I would derive that even one who slaughters [animals consecrated for] Temple maintenance outside is liable to karet, for they are called an offering, as it is stated: “And we have brought the Lord’s offering etc.: articles of gold, armlets and bracelets,” which were for the work of the Tabernacle.
rashi:b16.1: That is not fit for the entrance of the Tent of Meeting: such as items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which are not fit to come to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, since they are blemished animals, as we said above: one who assigns unblemished animals to Temple maintenance transgresses a prohibition.
rashi:b17.1: I exclude these, but not the red heifer of purification: the red heifer, that if he slaughtered it outside, not in its prescribed manner, not on its pyre, he would be liable to karet; and likewise the scapegoat, if he slaughtered it outside he would be liable to karet, since they are unblemished: for with the heifer it is written (Numbers 19:2), “in which there is no blemish,” and the scapegoat we include above, that it may not have a blemish.
rashi:b17.2: These are excluded: evidently it is to exclude the scapegoat.
rashi:b18.1: There: where “to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting” includes all consecrated unblemished animals, to make one liable for them outside, why do I need “unto the Lord” further? It is certainly to exclude.
rashi:b18.2: But here, where “fire” is to exclude: with regard to blemished animals it is written (Leviticus 22), “nor make an offering by fire of them etc.,” which implies: for what goes up to the fires, one who consecrates it blemished is liable on account of “you shall not consecrate,” but what does not go up to the fires, not; and the scapegoat is excluded. Therefore, why do I need “unto the Lord” to exclude, when it was already excluded by “fire”? Rather, it is certainly to include.
rashi:b19.1: It is permitted: to consecrate it.
rashi:b19.2: But the lottery: of [the goat for] the Name establishes only what is fit for the Name, for when he brings [the goats] and holds the lottery, he does not know on which of them the lot for the Name will come up. Therefore, perforce, we require both to be unblemished; so why do I need the verse?
rashi:b23.1: Such as where it became blemished: after the lottery, and he desacralized it onto its fellow, which is also blemished. And it teaches us that the one who desacralized it is flogged because he consecrated a blemished animal. And that is why it speaks of desacralizing: for if he had not desacralized it onto a blemished animal, there would be no lashes for “you shall not consecrate” on the second.
tosafot:b17.1: In brief: Rashi in Yoma, chapter Shenei Se’irei (Yoma 63b), says the words “red heifer of purification” should not be read in this baraita. The mishna in the last chapter of Zevaḥim (112a) exempts one who burns the red heifer outside its pit or sacrifices the scapegoat outside, “as it is stated: ‘and has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting’ — whatever is not fit for the entrance of the Tent of Meeting,” and the Gemara there challenges only from the scapegoat, citing this baraita. Had the baraita named the red heifer, the Gemara could have challenged from the heifer as well, and the answer given there does not fit the heifer. Tosafot then ask about the answer in Zevaḥim, “Here before the lottery, here after the lottery”: it implies that before the lottery, when the scapegoat is fit for the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, the verse still exempts one who sacrifices it outside, yet a baraita in Yoma (62b) says explicitly that before the lottery one who slaughters it outside is liable. They answer that by the conclusion in Zevaḥim, “Here before the confession, here after the confession,” both cases may be after the lottery, while before the lottery one may indeed be liable for slaughtering it outside, as in Yoma. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b23.1: Why do I need the verse? Such as where it became blemished after the lottery and he desacralized it onto its fellow: and that one too is blemished. And it teaches us that the one who desacralized it is flogged, because he consecrated it blemished. And that is why it speaks of desacralizing: for if he had not desacralized it onto a blemished one, there would be no lashes for “you shall not consecrate” on the second.
gershom:b1.1: For Rava, who says it is never effective, he returns [the interest].
gershom:b2.1: This one who was owed money by another, and the interest had already risen, so that he owed him four zuz of interest, and the borrower gave the lender [in their place] …
gershom:b3.1: A cloak worth five for four: when we repossess etc. Evidently Abaye holds that we repossess it from him. Rather, Abaye and Rava disagree with regard to whether a change acquires: that is, a change by which one transgressed the statement of the Merciful One, deviating from His command — for Abaye it acquires, that is, it is effective; for Rava it does not. Another version: they disagree [about these answers with regard to change] that we gave, that Abaye says it is effective and answers according to his reasoning, [and Rava says it is not effective and answers according to his reasoning]. This too is the “acquires” it speaks of, only that this version explains it [more fully].
gershom:b4.1: [Rather, with regard to what] do they disagree? With regard to whether a change acquires, as we said.
gershom:b5.1: [From where do we derive a transient blemish?] Since it could have said, “that which has a blemish… shall not be acceptable,” and it wrote “whatever [kol],” to include an animal with a transient blemish.
gershom:b6.1: “You shall not offer” is also not needed [for this], for if it comes for the prohibition against slaughtering a blemished animal, that is already stated below, as is explained further on, that slaughtering a blemished animal is derived from another verse.
gershom:b7.1: [For the prohibition against consecrating: for this “you shall not offer” is interpreted further on as “you shall not consecrate.”]
gershom:b8.1: And for burning all of it and for burning part of it: whether he burns all of it or burns part of it, he transgresses the prohibition “you shall not burn.”
gershom:b9.1: If [it is for] the prohibition against consecrating, that is already stated above, as we said, that this “whatever has a blemish you shall not offer” means “you shall not consecrate.”
gershom:b10.1: “Offering by fire [isheh]”: these are the fires, that is, the prohibition against burning.
gershom:b11.1: “Unto the Lord,” to include the scapegoat: [with regard to a blemished animal, that one may not bring a blemished one,] even though it does not go to the Lord. [But] the lottery establishes only what is fit for the Name; that is to say, even for the scapegoat we require [an unblemished animal].
gershom:b12.1: [But isn’t it taught: “offering”: this that is written, “and has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, to present it as an offering” — I would understand that even items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which are called an offering, if one slaughtered them outside, he would be liable.
gershom:b13.1: I exclude these: items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which are also blemished animals, as we say further on that one consecrates for Temple maintenance only blemished animals; but I do not exclude the red heifer of purification and the scapegoat, which are unblemished and fit for the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.]
gershom:b14.1: The verse states “unto the Lord”: those that are exclusively the Lord’s, for sacrifice — for them one is liable on account of slaughtering outside. These are excluded, the red heifer of purification and the scapegoat, which are not exclusively for sacrifice. Evidently “unto the Lord” is to exclude. [Here,] why do I need “unto the Lord”? Learn from it: what is “fire”? [What it includes is whatever effects atonement like the fires] to the Name: it is forbidden with a blemish. And the scapegoat too effects atonement, to Azazel, like the fires to the Name; therefore we require an unblemished animal.
gershom:b15.1: Rava said: it was necessary to write “unto the Lord” only for where the scapegoat became blemished after it was selected by lottery, and he desacralized it onto another goat that is blemished. Granted, initially, before they were selected by lottery, we require that both be unblemished, since we do not know which will be designated for the Name. But here, when it became blemished after the lottery, since the one for the Name is recognizable as unblemished, I would say he is not flogged when he brings the other, blemished one. It teaches us. Another version: the reason is that the verse wrote “unto the Lord” etc.
gershom:b16.1: Rav Yosef said: Whose is this [baraita], for which “unto the Lord” was needed to include? It is Ḥanan the Egyptian, who said: even [if the blood of the goat for the Name] is in the cup [and has not yet been sprinkled, and the scapegoat was lost or became blemished, he brings another as a partner, as the scapegoat].
gershom:b17.1: And pairs it: with this goat that was slaughtered; that is to say, he brings it without a lottery, since he cannot hold a lottery, as its fellow has already been slaughtered. And just as he can bring it without a lottery according to Ḥanan, one might think he can also bring a blemished one; that is why it was needed.
gershom:b18.1: And still, why is it needed [according to Ḥanan]?
gershom:b20.1: [Who said: even if the blood is in the cup, he brings another and pairs it with it. He says this to teach us that it is not deferred: the slaughtered one, so long as its blood has not been sprinkled, has a remedy even though its fellow died or was lost, and he brings another and pairs it with it. But that he brings it without a lottery — did you hear that from him? Perhaps he means he brings and holds a lottery. And how does he do it? He brings two and holds a lottery over them; the one whose lot comes up for the Name he sets aside, and the one whose lot comes up for Azazel he brings and pairs with the first one, whose blood is in the cup. And since he requires a lottery for them, he also requires it to be unblemished, since the lottery establishes only what is fit for the Name.]
gershom:b21.1: Whose is this, for which “unto the Lord” was needed to include? It is Rabbi Shimon, who said he brings its fellow without a lottery. One might think: just as it does not require a lottery, so too it should not require an unblemished animal. It teaches us.
gershom:b22.1: [The printed edition’s note: It seems that our Rabbi read in the Gemara: “Granted that you heard Rabbi Shimon say that it does not require a lottery, etc. Rather, Rava said, etc.,” and on this our Rabbi explained “and why would it occur to us, etc.”; and see Rashi here, who also cites this reading and rejects it.] And why would it occur to us that it does not require an unblemished animal? Granted that we do not require a lottery for the fellow that he brings now, since he already held a lottery over it at the outset, over the one that died and the one for the Name — but rather it is because [the printed note suggests: so as not to disqualify the second one, the one still standing] we require the second one [to remain fit]: for if you require a lottery for the one he brings, that implies the first lottery is void, and the one still standing, which did not die, would be disqualified. Therefore [no] further lottery is required; otherwise, Rabbi Shimon would have held that a lottery is required. And since a lottery would be required, he does not bring a blemished one, [for] whatever requires a lottery must be unblemished. [The Hebrew here is uncertain; this follows the printed corrections.]
gershom:b23.1: Rather, Rava said: it was needed for this, for example where the scapegoat became blemished after it was selected by lottery and he desacralized it onto another, etc. Rather, Ravina said: “unto the Lord” was needed to include, and it does not come for this, as you said, to include the scapegoat with regard to a blemished animal; rather, it comes to include the scapegoat with regard to [an animal] lacking in time. And with what are we dealing here? Where the one who sold the scapegoat had a dangerously ill person in his house, and he slaughtered the scapegoat’s mother on Yom Kippur for the needs of the sick person. One might think that its offspring, which is for Azazel, is not subject to slaughter, and so its death at Azazel should not be forbidden on account of the prohibition “it and its young you shall not slaughter in one day.” “Unto the Lord” teaches us to include it, that it is forbidden, for they say in the West [the Land of Israel]: pushing it off the cliff is its slaughter, and it is forbidden. [The printed edition’s note: up to here belongs to the previous page.]
